value: Can a nature-of-science course built on anomalous events produce the conceptual change that lets science-trained pre-service teachers distinguish evidence from inference and use models to predict, and what does the result imply for teacher preparation and standards?

Reports five years of a graduate nature-of-science course in which science-major teaching candidates scored ~91% on algorithmic density questions but ~49% on conceptual floating-and-sinking questions and, even after twelve hours of instruction, almost never invoked Archimedes' principle in a new demonstration, which the authors use to argue that pre-service programmes and national standards overestimate what algorithm-trained students understand.

quote: During a five-year period the authors taught over 100 students in a graduate course (The Nature of Science) counting toward teacher certification at the Harvard Graduate School of Education.

We examine the deceptive belief that student success with algorithms and word problems leads to conceptual understanding as well as the conceptual change necessary to understand the relationship between evidence and inference as explored in the nature of science course.
